documents.text:
Gracias Por Invitar · Living Project Portal 
 Gracias Por Invitar , Living Project Portal, Sprint 1
 Market Research
 Five candidate problems, 51 customer interviews in two phases, and how the team narrowed to one.
 Version 1.1 , Draft for team review , revised Sep 15, 2026 Owner To be assigned Team Samuel Alderete, Jazmin Huerta, Christian Lopez-Matulessy, Emmanuel Saenz, Oscar Vargas Course CS 4390/5388 Software Project Management , The University of Texas at El Paso , Fall 2026 Web https://gpi-portal.onrender.com/sprint-1/market-research/ Draft for team review This synthesis was drafted with AI assistance from the team's own interview sheets; see the AI use disclosure on the Sprint 1 page. Every count below comes from the 51 sheets in the interview evidence . The team reviews, edits and approves this document before it is marked final, and the section on the pivot from Candidate 2 in particular needs the team's own words.

 Summary

 The team started Sprint 1 with five candidate problems and talked to 51 people about them in two phases. Phase 1 (26 interviews across all five) cut the field to two. Phase 2 (25 interviews on the survivors) reversed the Phase 1 ranking: the nutrition candidate that had looked strongest did not hold up under a broader sample, and the events candidate that had looked weak sharpened into a specific, repeated ask. The project the team is taking forward is Candidate 3: a single place to see what is happening in El Paso, before it happens. 

 Three patterns showed up across everything the team researched, not just the winner. Anything that depends on daily manual logging dies within weeks. The pain people can actually describe is finding out too late, whether it is a protein shortfall at 10 pm, a concert that already happened, or a rental fee for a film they already had. And where a free incumbent already works well enough, people do not want another app.

 How the research was done

 The method was customer discovery under Mom Test rules: ask about the last time something happened, not whether an idea sounds good; never pitch; record participants by role, never by name. Each conversation went on a guided sheet with a body of five or six questions, follow-up probes, verbatim quotes and a one-sentence takeaway written within 24 hours.

 Phase When Interviews Candidates Who 
 Phase 1 Sep 3 to 7 26 All five (5, 5, 6, 5, 5) Emmanuel Saenz (C1), Samuel Alderete (C2), Jazmin Huerta (C3), Oscar Vargas (C4), Christian Lopez-Matulessy (C5) 
 Scoping checkpoint Sep 8 Cut to two: Candidates 2 and 3 Team 
 Phase 2 Sep 9 25 Candidate 2 (13), Candidate 3 (12) Oscar Vargas, Jazmin Huerta, Christian Lopez-Matulessy (C2); Samuel Alderete, Emmanuel Saenz, Jazmin Huerta (C3) 

 Participants were reached in person: on the UTEP campus, at gyms, outside a construction site, at a restaurant and a bar, at a county courthouse, and, for Candidate 1, in Fort Worth. Everyone consented to notes and to a later follow-up.

 Aggregate findings

 1. Manual logging dies within weeks, in every category we tested

 This was the one finding that crossed candidate lines. In the finance conversations, three of five people had started a spreadsheet or template and stopped inside a month ("by the third week I ended up getting lazy and just stopped"). In nutrition, all five Phase 1 participants had quit a tracking app within one to four weeks, and four of the five Phase 2 participants who had tried an app had quit it too, over exams, forgotten snacks, or homemade food they could not estimate. The people who kept going were the ones who had removed the logging: the contractor with a spreadsheet he built himself, the nurse with cash envelopes, the meal-prepper who eats the same five lunches.

 The implication for any candidate: a product that needs the user to enter things every day inherits this churn on day one.

 2. The pain people can describe is finding out too late

 When participants were asked for the last time something went wrong, the stories had the same shape across three candidates. The construction worker "checks at night and I'm still 700 or 800 calories under." The student who "found out about a car show after seeing people's pictures from it that night." The person who rented Dune 2 for six dollars and "found out later it was on Max, which my girlfriend pays for." The feeling is the same: the information existed, and it arrived after the moment it was useful.

 3. The information exists; it does not reach people

 For events specifically, nobody said El Paso lacks things to do. They said they do not hear about them. Announcements live on the Instagram pages of the venue, the organizer, or an aggregator account like FitFam, and only reach the people already following the right ones. "Unless you follow the exact business or page hosting it, you might never see it." People without social media, or who use it lightly, are cut off almost entirely: "since I don't have social media, I don't have an easy way to get to this information."

 4. A free incumbent that works beats a better idea

 Where a good-enough free tool existed, participants used it and felt no problem. The engineer's credit card already categorizes purchases. Three Phase 2 nutrition participants find MyFitnessPal encouraging and sufficient. The streaming problem, the one with the strongest evidence of wasted money, is already served by JustWatch and Reelgood at no cost. This is why Candidate 5 was dropped despite its evidence, and it is a bar Candidate 3 has to clear: for the heavy Instagram user with a curated feed, "Instagram already puts everything in one feed for me, so it doesn't really bother me."

 5. Questions about opinions produce opinions

 The Candidate 4 (investing education) interviews are the clearest lesson in method. The questions asked what people knew, feared and would want, and every answer was a hypothetical: "I think if it can clearly explain things to beginners I would try it out." Not one participant described a past attempt to invest or learn. The candidate was dropped less for a weak market than for evidence that could not have disconfirmed anything.

 Top pick: Candidate 3, an events hub for El Paso

 What we tested

 The problem statement as written on the sheets: people find it hard to find events and places to go to in El Paso/Juárez, often finding out after the events have already happened. 

 Phase 1: a real problem, a weak signal

 Six conversations. All six could name an event they had missed, which put the problem on the board. But only two of six said it happens often, and three said they do not look for events at all; things arrive through a feed or a friend or a spouse. Two of the six described finding events easy once they had followed enough accounts. Ranked against Candidate 2's five-for-five Phase 1, this looked like the weaker survivor, and the team carried it into Phase 2 mainly because the missed-event stories were so specific.

 Phase 2: the signal sharpened

 The Phase 2 question set was tightened around past behavior: the last public event you attended and how you heard about it, where you look for details, the last time you found out too late and how often that happens, and one open question about what you would change. Twelve conversations, six of them with working professionals rather than students.

 # Participant How often they find out too late What they would change 
 1 UTEP student, regular at markets and concerts Once or twice a month One place to see everything happening that weekend 
 2 College student who plans weekends with friends "Pretty often" Hearing about things at least a week ahead 
 3 UTEP student who goes out often "Enough that I've noticed" El Paso and Juárez together; discovery beyond what the feed already shows 
 4 Student with limited social media use Every couple of months Events by date, without needing Instagram 
 5 Student with a heavily curated Instagram feed Rarely (recorded as a weak signal) Filtering by type of event 
 6 Software specialist Could not say: "I'm not aware of them" Tell it your interests, have it tell you what is on 
 7 Social worker A few times a year (sold-out concert, full race registration) A standardized source, though "how would people find out about it" 
 8 Attorney A couple of times Advertising beyond social media 
 9 County worker Never; a spouse finds their events No suggestion 
 10 Victim advocate About once a year (tickets gone by the time they hear) A weekly round-up or calendar from official accounts 
 11 Paralegal Rarely; follows enough accounts One source; an interest-based email digest 
 12 Aerospace engineer, regular event-goer At least once a month, "every three weeks on average" A central listing, like the weekly page that used to exist and stopped 

 Read strictly: six of twelve miss events they would have attended on a recurring basis (monthly, to a few times a year), four say rarely, and two gave no usable frequency. That is not everyone, and the document should not claim it is. What did converge was the answer to the open question. Seven of twelve, in their own words and without being offered the idea, asked for a single place to see what is coming: "there isn't one place where I can just see everything happening that weekend"; "El Paso lacks a one-source location"; "there used to be a page that would put all of the events that were going on every week, but they stopped doing that." Three asked for interest-based filtering. Two asked for lead time of about a week. Two asked for reach beyond social media.

 Who is underserved

 Three groups fell out of both phases.

 People who rely on word of mouth. They hear about things from a cousin, a classmate, a spouse, and they are the ones who find out from the photos. This is the largest group in the sample and the one with the strongest stories.

 People with little or no social media. Two Phase 2 participants and one Phase 1 participant. Google gives them "tourist attractions or places that are always open instead of actual events happening that weekend." The attorney's fix was a sign by the road. They are the clearest gap in what exists today.

 People with a curated feed who want less noise, not more. They find events easily and would use filtering by interest. They are the least likely early adopters and the strongest reminder that a feed is the incumbent to beat.

 Where people look today, and where it fails

 Channel What it does well Where it fails, in participants' words 
 Instagram and TikTok Everything is posted there, eventually Only shows what you already follow; "keeps showing me the same type of stuff"; useless without an account 
 FitFam and similar aggregator accounts One place many locals check Still one account's curation; participants who did not follow it did not know it existed 
 Facebook events Notifies when friends are going Skewed to whoever posts there; fading among students 
 Google Finds details once you know the name Returns places, not events: "it doesn't really show me everything that's actually happening" 
 Ticketmaster, artist accounts Big shows Only big shows, and only if you follow the artist; tickets gone before you hear 
 Flyers, QR codes, road signs Reach people offline Localized to one coffee shop's wall or one road 
 A weekly listing page (now defunct) Exactly what people asked for It stopped 

 What the evidence does not support

 That everyone has this problem. Four of twelve Phase 2 participants rarely miss events, and the heavy Instagram user is satisfied. The pitch is for the underserved groups above, not for everyone in El Paso.

 That Juárez is in scope. Participants split. One wants both sides together in one place; another does not cross at all ("I feel it's still too violent"). Six of the twelve interviews describe El Paso venues only. This is an open scoping question for the charter, not a settled fact.

 That the sample represents the city. Twelve people, half of them students, interviewed on one day. Phase 1's six Candidate 3 sheets do not record who was interviewed or where.

 What didn't work, and what we pivoted from

 Candidate 1: money already spoken for (dropped after Phase 1)

 Five interviews in Fort Worth. Three participants had abandoned manual expense logging, which is real, but nobody described the stated problem of not knowing how much income was already committed. Two of the five had no financial pain at all and said so. The evidence pointed at a different problem than the one on the sheet, and one that budgeting apps already fight over.

 Candidate 4: Market Master (dropped after Phase 1)

 See finding 5. Five participants, five sets of hypotheticals, no past behavior. Dropped for the quality of what could be learned as much as for the market.

 Candidate 5: searching across streaming services (dropped after Phase 1)

 The strongest Phase 1 evidence of any candidate: three of five had paid to rent or buy something a service they already subscribed to carried, and all five described giving up on choosing something to watch. Dropped anyway, on scope and incumbents. Availability data across five services is not obtainable by a student team, and JustWatch and Reelgood already do the search for free. Good evidence for a problem the team could not build a defensible answer to.

 Candidate 2: eating toward a body goal (ranked first after Phase 1, dropped after Phase 2)

 Phase 1 made this the favorite: all five participants had quit macro tracking within four weeks, all five described finding out at the end of the day that they had fallen short (40 grams of protein; 700 to 800 calories; enough calories but almost no protein), and all five named advance meal preparation as what made their best week work. It also scored best on scope (arithmetic over a food database) and on monetization (a proven category). The team recorded one limitation at the time: every participant had been recruited because they already tracked macros, so the sample could confirm the problem but could not disconfirm it.

 Phase 2 fixed the sample and the problem did not survive it. Of thirteen participants, three had never or barely tracked, three tracked loosely, two long-term app users find MyFitnessPal encouraging and sufficient, and four had tracked and quit for the logging-burden reasons in finding 1. Not one described the specific problem on the sheet, not being able to tell in advance whether the day's meals would hit the target. What recurred instead was logging burden, which is exactly the ground MyFitnessPal and MacroFactor already compete on, and the churn the team's own Phase 1 had demonstrated (five of five quit) would be the team's churn too.

 The team also weighed positioning. Candidate 2 is a proven but crowded category, and inside the course it was the consensus pick among several teams, which left no room to differentiate. Candidate 3 was a problem the team found more interesting to work on, and in a semester project that matters for the quality of the work.

 Team input needed The paragraph above states the team's reasoning as relayed for this draft. Confirm it, correct it, or replace it with the team's own account before this document is marked final. Be ready to defend it in the final Q&A.

 What the method got wrong, and what changed

 Phase 1 grid sheets. Candidates 3, 4 and 5 were captured in a question-by-interview grid with no interviewer, date, role or one-sentence takeaway per conversation. The answers are there; the synthesis is not. Phase 2 used one guided sheet per interview for everything, which is why its evidence is stronger.

 Question design between phases. The Candidate 3 questions were rewritten around "the last time" and "how often," which produced the frequency table above. The Candidate 2 questions moved the other way, toward "have you found tracking encouraging or discouraging," and produced more feelings than stories. Some of the weaker Phase 2 nutrition signal may be the questions rather than the market.

 Geography. Six Phase 2 interviews record their location as a county courthouse without naming the city. The participants describe El Paso venues and events, but the sheets should say so.

 The per-person floor. The assignment asked for at least five interviews per member. In Phase 2 the team distributed 25 across two candidates and one member finished with four.

 One answer, five directions. The open "change one thing" question produced five different product directions: aggregation, lead time, combining El Paso and Juárez, a date view without Instagram, and interest filters. Aggregation was the most common and is the core; the rest are scoping decisions for the charter.

 Open questions carried into the charter

 Is Juárez in scope for the first version, or is this an El Paso product first?

 Where do the events come from: organizer submissions, curation by the team, or scraping public posts? Participant 7's question stands: how would people find out about the place that lists everything?

 Which underserved group is first: word-of-mouth dependents, or people without social media?

 What lead time is the product promising? Participants said about a week.

 Which categories on day one? The sample mentioned markets, car meets and card shows, concerts, comedy, races, trivia nights and kermeses.

 Generated from the portal source at build time. The web page and this PDF are two renders of the same document. Revision history: v1.0 (Sep 10, 2026) First synthesis of both interview phases, for team review.; v1.1 (Sep 15, 2026) Phase 1 interviewers for Candidates 3, 4 and 5 added from the team's record; the grid sheets did not carry them.

documents.text:
Gracias Por Invitar · Living Project Portal 
 Gracias Por Invitar , Living Project Portal, Sprint 1
 Business Strategy
 The strategy-to-project chain: why this project earns the right to exist and what objective it serves.
 Version 0.1 , Draft for team review , revised Sep 10, 2026 Owner To be assigned Team Samuel Alderete, Jazmin Huerta, Christian Lopez-Matulessy, Emmanuel Saenz, Oscar Vargas Course CS 4390/5388 Software Project Management , The University of Texas at El Paso , Fall 2026 Web https://gpi-portal.onrender.com/sprint-1/business-strategy/ Draft for team review The chain below is drafted from the Sprint 1 research. The business objective and its measures are the team's to set; a candidate framing is offered for comparison, not as a decision. The go/no-go recommendation belongs to the Sprint 2 business case and is the team's own work.

 The chain in one view

 Link Gracias Por Invitar 
 Market signal Events in El Paso are announced across dozens of social accounts; people hear about them from the people who happened to follow the right one, and often from the photos afterward. 
 Problem People find out about events after they have already happened. 
 Opportunity Nobody serves the whole city in one place. A weekly listing page used to, and participants still miss it. 
 Business objective Draft, below: become the place El Paso checks first for what is happening this week. 
 Project An events hub for El Paso: one listing, by date, from arena concerts to farmers markets and car meets. 
 Success measures Draft, below. 

 Why this project earns the right to exist

 The problem is real for a defined group. In Phase 2, six of twelve people described missing events they would have attended on a recurring basis, and seven of twelve, asked an open question about what they would change, asked for a single place to see what is coming. The people it fails hardest are the ones who rely on word of mouth and the ones with little or no social media. See the Market Research for the counts.

 The incumbents are not built for this job. Instagram shows people what they already follow. Google returns places, not events. Ticketmaster covers big shows. FitFam is one account's curation, known to the people who know it. Each is good at its own job and none of them is a listing of what is happening in El Paso this weekend.

 Demand for the specific shape has been demonstrated once already. One participant described a page that "would put all of the events that were going on every week," and that they used until it stopped. Another asked for "a weekly event round-up or calendar." The ask is not novel; it is unmet.

 It is buildable by this team in a semester. The core is a listing with dates and categories, not a recommendation engine. The hard part is sourcing events, and that is a process and partnership problem the team can plan, not a technology the team cannot obtain (which is what stopped Candidate 5).

 Who it serves first

 People who rely on word of mouth , the largest group in the sample and the one with the strongest stories. Give them the thing they currently get from the friend who follows everything.

 People with little or no social media. For them there is currently nothing except a sign by the road.

 Event organizers and venues , who today advertise only to their existing followers. They are the supply side and the likeliest partners.

 The heavy Instagram user with a curated feed is not the first customer. They are served well enough by what they have and they will judge the product against it.

 The business objective

 Team decision Candidate framing for comparison, drafted from the research: Within the semester, launch a public listing of events in El Paso that a defined group of residents checks weekly, measured by the number of events listed per week, the number of organizers submitting directly, and the share of visitors who return the following week. The team sets the actual objective, its horizon and its numbers. Replace this box with the agreed objective.

 Success measures (draft)

 Measure Why it matters Target 
 Events listed per week The product is only useful if it is more complete than a feed Team to set 
 Organizers submitting directly Sustainable supply, not team curation forever Team to set 
 Returning weekly visitors The habit the product is trying to create Team to set 
 Lead time of listed events Participants asked for about a week Team to set 

 How it could sustain itself

 Not decided in Sprint 1 and not claimed here. The options the research points at, listed neutrally for the Sprint 2 business case: organizer listings (free basic, paid featured), sponsorship by venues or the city's tourism office, and promoted events. Each one depends on supply the team has not secured yet, which is why sourcing events is the first strategic risk below.

 What would make the team stop

 Kill criteria, so the go/no-go in Sprint 2 has something to test against:

 Events cannot be sourced reliably enough to be more complete than a good Instagram feed.

 Organizers will not submit, and manual curation by the team does not scale past the semester.

 Visitors do not come back the following week.

 Strategic risks

 Risk Effect First response 
 Sourcing: the listing is thinner than a curated feed The product loses to the incumbent it is trying to replace Start with a small number of categories and venues and be complete in those 
 Discovery: "how would people find out about the standardized way" Nobody visits the hub Distribution plan with organizers and the accounts people already follow 
 Scope creep toward Juárez, filters, notifications The semester runs out before the listing exists Charter scope boundary; Juárez is an open question, not a feature 
 A free incumbent adds a city-wide listing The gap closes Speed, and organizer relationships that a platform does not have 

 Links

 Market Research : the evidence behind every claim above.

 Project Charter : scope boundary, assumptions and stakeholders.

documents.text:
Gracias Por Invitar · Living Project Portal 
 Gracias Por Invitar , Living Project Portal, Sprint 1
 Project Charter
 Scope boundary, assumptions, constraints, milestones and the stakeholder register.
 Version 0.1 , Draft for team review , revised Sep 10, 2026 Owner To be assigned Team Samuel Alderete, Jazmin Huerta, Christian Lopez-Matulessy, Emmanuel Saenz, Oscar Vargas Course CS 4390/5388 Software Project Management , The University of Texas at El Paso , Fall 2026 Web https://gpi-portal.onrender.com/sprint-1/project-charter/ Draft for team review The charter is the anchor document for every sprint after this one. The sections below carry the facts on record (team, dates, problem statement, research findings). Sections marked for team input need decisions only the team can make. Nothing marked as a draft should survive to the final version.

 Project purpose

 Gracias Por Invitar is a centralized hub for events in El Paso, from official events such as concerts and festivals to local ones such as farmers markets, car meets and card shows. Its purpose is that people find out about events before they happen instead of after. The name is the problem: "thanks for the invite" is what you say when the photos show up and nobody told you.

 The project exists to satisfy the business objective set out in the Business Strategy , and it is being managed and documented sprint by sprint on this portal for CS 4390/5388 at The University of Texas at El Paso.

 Problem statement

 As tested in Sprint 1: people find it hard to find events and places to go to in El Paso/Juárez, often finding out after the events have already happened. 

 As refined by the research: people in El Paso find out about events after they have already happened, because announcements are scattered across dozens of social accounts and only reach the people already following the right ones. The Market Research holds the evidence.

 Objectives

 Team decision Draft objectives for the team to confirm, cut or replace. They mirror the success measures in the Business Strategy.

 Publish a public listing of events in El Paso, by date and category, that is more complete within its chosen categories than any single social account.

 Give organizers a way to submit events directly, so the listing does not depend on the team's own curation.

 Reach the two underserved groups the research identified: people who rely on word of mouth, and people with little or no social media.

 Keep a complete, public record of how the project is managed, on this portal, every sprint.

 Scope boundary

 In scope

 Events in El Paso, Texas.

 Both official and local events: concerts, festivals, sports, markets, car meets, card shows, comedy, races, trivia nights, kermeses and similar public gatherings.

 A date-first view: what is happening today, this weekend, this week.

 Categories and interest-based filtering, since three Phase 2 participants asked for it.

 A way for organizers to submit events.

 Lead time: events listed at least about a week ahead where the organizer's own announcement allows it.

 Out of scope

 Ticketing, payments, or reselling.

 Social features: comments, RSVPs visible to friends, messaging.

 Private events and invitations.

 Organizer tooling beyond submission (no CRM, no analytics dashboards) in the first version.

 Recommendation or personalization engines. Filters are in scope; prediction is not.

 Open scoping questions

 Team decision These came out of the research and need a decision before Sprint 2 estimates anything.

 Juárez. Participants split: one wants both sides in one place, one does not cross at all, and most described El Paso only. The current boundary is El Paso; Juárez is a decision, not an assumption.

 Sourcing. Organizer submissions, team curation, public posts, or a mix. This decides the product's effort profile more than any feature.

 First categories. Which categories the listing is complete in on day one.

 First group served. Word-of-mouth dependents or people without social media.

 Deliverables

 Management record (this portal), every sprint. Sprint 1: Market Research, Business Strategy, Project Charter, interview evidence. Sprint 2: business case, estimation appendix, ROI analysis, change log. Later sprints as released by the course. Every public document exists as a web page and as a PDF, and the private retrospective goes to Blackboard only.

 Product. 

 Team decision Define the product deliverable for the semester: a working web application, a prototype, or a plan and estimate only. The course guidelines describe the portal as the major deliverable; what the team commits to building is the team's call and drives every estimate in Sprint 2.

 Assumptions

 Team review Drafted from the research. Each one is a thing the project will be wrong about if it is false; keep the ones the team believes and add the rest.

 Event information for El Paso is publicly available (organizer posts, venue pages, city listings) and can be collected legitimately.

 Organizers want more reach than their own followers and will submit events to a listing that gives it to them.

 A weekly habit is possible: people will check one place for what is happening, as they once did with the listing page that stopped.

 About a week of lead time is enough for most participants' planning, per Phase 2.

 The team can build and run the listing on free or already-available hosting for the length of the semester.

 The five team members remain available for the semester at the effort the course expects.

 Constraints

 Schedule. Six sprints, each two weeks, deadlines fixed by the course (see milestones). Nothing slips.

 Team. Five students, part time, with other coursework.

 Budget. No project budget. Hosting for the portal must be free; product infrastructure is limited to free tiers and what the team already has.

 Public record. Everything except the retrospective and peer evaluations is public, sprint by sprint, and earlier pages are never replaced.

 AI use. Permitted for the website and for drafts the team reviews; not permitted for the individual reflections, the estimation memo, or any go/no-go reasoning. Every sprint carries a disclosure.

 Stakeholder register

 Stakeholder Type Interest Influence How they are engaged 
 Samuel Alderete Team Delivery of the project and the portal High Team member; role to be added 
 Jazmin Huerta Team Delivery of the project and the portal High Team member; role to be added 
 Christian Lopez-Matulessy Team Delivery of the project and the portal High Team member; role to be added 
 Emmanuel Saenz Team Delivery of the project and the portal High Team member; role to be added 
 Oscar Vargas Team Delivery of the project and the portal High Team member; role to be added 
 Course instructor, CS 4390/5388 Sponsor and evaluator A well-managed project with a complete, defensible record High Sprint demos, portal reviews, Blackboard submissions 
 Peer teams Reviewers Gallery-walk feedback on Sprint 1 Low Portal Debut Day feedback and the team's written response 
 Event-goers who rely on word of mouth Customer Finding out before, not after Medium Interviewed in Sprint 1; follow-up consent on record 
 Event-goers with little or no social media Customer A source that does not require an account Medium Interviewed in Sprint 1; follow-up consent on record 
 Organizers and venues Supplier and customer Reach beyond their own followers High Not yet engaged; sourcing decision pending 
 Incumbent channels (Instagram, TikTok, Facebook, FitFam, Google, Ticketmaster) Environment None in the project High on the market Understood through the research; possible distribution partners 
 City of El Paso and its tourism accounts Environment, possible partner Visibility of official events Medium Not yet engaged 

 Team input needed Add roles for each team member, and any stakeholder the team knows of that the research did not surface (a faculty advisor, a venue contact, a student organization).

 Milestones

 Sprint Block Due Contents 
 1 Aug 25 to Sep 21 Mon, Sep 21, 2026, 11:59 PM Market Research, Business Strategy, Project Charter, evidence 
 2 Sep 22 to Oct 5 Mon, Oct 5, 2026, 11:59 PM Business case, estimation appendix, ROI, change log 
 3 Oct 6 to Oct 19 Mon, Oct 19, 2026, 11:59 PM To be released 
 4 Oct 20 to Nov 2 Mon, Nov 2, 2026, 11:59 PM To be released 
 5 Nov 3 to Nov 16 Mon, Nov 16, 2026, 11:59 PM To be released 
 6 Nov 17 to Nov 30 Mon, Nov 30, 2026, 11:59 PM To be released 

 Portal Debut Day is Tuesday, September 22. The final class session is Tuesday, December 1.

 Initial risks

 Team review A starting register, drafted from the research and the constraints. The full risk register is developed in later sprints.

 Risk Likelihood Impact Response 
 Events cannot be sourced completely enough to beat a curated feed High High Decide sourcing first; start narrow and be complete in a few categories 
 Nobody finds the hub (the discovery problem, one level up) High High Distribution through organizers and the accounts people already follow 
 Scope grows toward Juárez, notifications, personalization Medium High Hold the scope boundary; changes go through the change log 
 Uneven contribution across five members Medium Medium Ownership named per page and per document; contribution statements every sprint 
 Sprint deadlines are fixed and short Certain Medium Publish early; the portal is live before the deadline, not at it 

 Roles and responsibilities

 Team input needed Name who owns the portal, each document, the product work, and the Blackboard submissions. The guidelines require that every member can explain every page.

 Approval

 Role Name Date 
 Project team All five members Pending 
 Instructor acknowledgement Pending
